author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: PKD's first published novel (1955) imagines a future society that distributes supreme power by a rigged cosmic lottery and the ritual assassin licensed to kill whoever the wheel elevates—an early, kinetic study of how systems of chance and control organize a whole civilization.
page_summary:
In a 2203 governed by 'Minimax' game theory, social position is assigned by a lottery of 'bottles' that can, in principle, twitch anyone into the role of Quizmaster, the world's ruler. The system pairs each Quizmaster with a legally sanctioned assassin, so that power is always held under threat of sudden death. Ted Benteley, a biochemist who swears fealty just as the old Quizmaster is displaced, is drawn into the intrigue around the new ruler Reese Verrick and the telepathic corps that guards him, while a separate strand chases the legend of a tenth planet.

The novel already carries PKD's signature suspicion of authority: power here is a machine of chance and surveillance, legitimated by ritual and defended by a telepath-staffed apparatus that reads minds to prevent assassination. Loyalty, oaths, and the manipulation of a supposedly fair game become the real substance of politics. The prose is faster and pulpier than his mature work, but the preoccupation—how impersonal systems assign worth and constrain freedom—is fully present.

As the book that launched his career as a novelist, Solar Lottery marks the start of a corpus obsessed with the operation of control. It was published in 1955 by Ace, the first of the many Ace paperbacks that carried his early science fiction.

biography_events.event: Publishes debut novel Solar Lottery through Ace Books as paperback original
